cards.back: Mechanism of injury: the forces and way an injury occurred (e.g., rollover, fall height, penetrating object). Guides index of suspicion and trauma center decisions.
Study of how motion and energy transfer cause injury. Kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x velocity squared, so speed matters more than mass.
Goal of definitive surgical care within about 60 minutes of injury. Platinum 10 minutes: limit scene time for critical trauma to 10 min or less.
Body in motion stays in motion until acted on by an outside force (e.g., a stopped car, then the occupant hits the dash).

cards.front: Three collisions in a vehicle crash
cards.back: 1) Vehicle hits object. 2) Occupant hits the vehicle interior. 3) Internal organs hit the body wall/skeleton.
Your anticipation of possible injuries based on MOI, even without obvious signs.

cards.front: Penetrating trauma: low vs high energy
cards.back: Knife = low energy (damage along path). Handgun = medium. Rifle = high energy with cavitation and wide tissue damage.
Scene size-up, spinal motion restriction as needed, general impression, then control life-threatening hemorrhage first, then airway, breathing, circulation, disability, expose.
DCAP-BTLS: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures/Penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling.

cards.front: Which trauma patients get a rapid trauma assessment?
cards.back: Significant MOI or unresponsive/altered patients get a full-body rapid exam. Isolated injury with minor MOI gets a focused exam.
About 5 to 6 liters (approx. 70 mL/kg). Child about 80 mL/kg; infants lose volume quickly, so small losses matter.
Direct pressure, then pressure dressing, then tourniquet (or hemostatic gauze packing) for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled. Per local protocol.
Place 2-3 inches above the wound (proximal), not over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops and distal pulse is gone. Write time applied. Do not loosen.
Pack firmly into wound (junctional areas such as groin/axilla/neck) and hold direct pressure at least 3 minutes (follow product directions).
Sit patient leaning forward, pinch the soft part of the nose 10 minutes. Suspect head injury if after trauma; avoid pinching with skull fracture/CSF.
Inadequate delivery of oxygen and nutrients to tissues because of poor perfusion. Cells shift to anaerobic metabolism.
Pump (heart), fluid (blood volume), and container (blood vessels).
Loss of blood or fluid volume (hemorrhage, burns, dehydration, vomiting/diarrhea). Most common shock in trauma.
Pump failure (heart attack, CHF). Often has pulmonary edema, JVD, and crackles.
Neurogenic, septic, anaphylactic: dilated vessels make the container too big.
Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism: blood flow physically blocked.
Spinal cord injury with loss of sympathetic tone: low BP, bradycardia, warm dry skin (below injury), and priapism possible.
Anxiety/restlessness, tachycardia, pale cool clammy skin, delayed cap refill, normal BP, tachypnea.
Falling blood pressure, altered mental status, weak/absent peripheral pulses, labored breathing, cyanosis, ashen skin.
Organ damage is permanent and death follows even if BP is restored.

cards.front: Early sign of shock in children
cards.back: Tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and altered mental status. Hypotension is a LATE sign (they compensate well, then crash).
Control bleeding, high-flow oxygen if hypoxic (maintain SpO2 94% or above), keep warm, supine, rapid transport. Avoid food/drink.
Arterial: bright red, spurting. Venous: dark red, steady flow. Capillary: slow oozing.
Adult about 1 liter, child about 500 mL, infant about 100-200 mL.
Signs of rising intracranial pressure: HYPERtension (widening pulse pressure), BRADYcardia, irregular respirations.
Bruising behind the ear over the mastoid; indicates basilar skull fracture (late sign).
Periorbital ecchymosis; indicates basilar skull fracture (can appear hours later).
Clear or pink fluid from ears or nose after head trauma; suggests skull fracture. Do not stop the flow; cover loosely.
4 spontaneous, 3 to voice, 2 to pain, 1 none.
5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none.
6 obeys commands, 5 localizes pain, 4 withdraws from pain, 3 flexion (decorticate), 2 extension (decerebrate), 1 none.
Range 3-15. Severe 8 or less, moderate 9-12, mild 13-15. 15 is normal. GCS 8 or less: airway at risk; BLS airway/BVM and request ALS (advanced airway is not EMT scope).
Decorticate: arms flexed toward core. Decerebrate: arms and legs extended (worse prognosis).
Declining mental status, vomiting, headache, unequal or sluggish pupils, posturing, Cushing's triad.
Maintain airway, oxygen to avoid hypoxia, avoid hyperventilation unless herniation signs (per local protocol), SMR, rapid transport.
Temporary altered brain function after a blow; may include confusion, amnesia, headache. No structural damage on CT.

cards.front: When to use spinal motion restriction
cards.back: MOI with altered mental status, neuro deficit, spine pain/tenderness, distracting injury or intoxication, per local protocol/selective criteria.
Collar limits neck movement; measure per manufacturer. Does not replace manual in-line stabilization until patient is secured.

cards.front: Airway-opening maneuver for a patient with suspected spinal injury
cards.back: Jaw-thrust maneuver without head tilt. If it does not open the airway, use head tilt-chin lift: a patent airway takes priority.
2 or more adjacent ribs fractured in 2 or more places, creating a free-floating segment.
Flail segment moves in on inhalation and out on exhalation. Give oxygen; assist with BVM if breathing is inadequate. Bulky-dressing stabilization only per local protocol.
Seal with occlusive dressing taped on 3 sides (or vented chest seal); watch for tension pneumothorax and burp dressing if worsening.
Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side.
Severe dyspnea, absent breath sounds, JVD, tracheal deviation (late), hypotension. Needle decompression is beyond EMT scope; rapid transport/ALS.
Blood in the pleural space; dull percussion, shock signs, decreased breath sounds. Rapid transport.
Blood in the pericardial sac compressing the heart; usually from penetrating trauma.
Hypotension, JVD, muffled (distant) heart tones. Signs of cardiac tamponade.
Severe chest compression: head/neck cyanosis, JVD, bulging eyes, petechiae. Treat ABCs, rapid transport.
Bruised lung tissue; delayed respiratory distress, hemoptysis.
Crepitus under skin from air leakage; sign of pneumothorax or airway injury.
Do not push organs back; cover with moist sterile saline dressing then occlusive covering. Keep warm, legs flexed if no contraindication.
Solid (liver, spleen, kidneys) bleed heavily. Hollow (stomach, intestines) leak contents causing peritonitis.
Rigid or distended abdomen, guarding, tenderness, Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain from spleen), bruising (Cullen/Grey Turner late).
Do not remove (except in cheek obstructing airway or interfering with CPR); stabilize with bulky dressings.
Suspect with MOI and pelvic pain; do not rock pelvis or compress repeatedly. Bind with pelvic binder/sheet per protocol; treat for shock.
Pulse, Motor function, Sensation: check distal to injury before AND after splinting.
Immobilize the joint above and below a long bone injury; the bone above and below a joint injury.
Reduce pain, prevent further tissue/vessel/nerve damage, limit bleeding.
Pulseless extremity or severely angulated; one gentle attempt, stop if resistance or pain increases (per local protocol). Do not realign joints.
Isolated mid-shaft femur fracture without pelvis, hip, knee, ankle injury (pain relief, bleeding control).
Open: bone ends or wound through skin; control bleeding, sterile dressing. Closed: skin intact.
Dislocation: bone out of joint. Sprain: ligament injury. Strain: muscle/tendon injury.
Pain out of proportion, tense swelling, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia, late: pulselessness (the 6 P's).
Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Wrap the cold pack in cloth; apply up to about 20 minutes at a time.
Control bleeding (tourniquet if needed); wrap part in moist sterile gauze, place in plastic bag, keep cool on ice; do not freeze or soak in water.
Epidermis only: red, dry, painful (sunburn). No blisters.
Epidermis + dermis: blisters, moist, red, very painful. Do not break blisters.
All skin layers: white, brown or charred, leathery, painless (nerve damage).
Head 9, each arm 9, chest 9 + abdomen 9 (front trunk 18), back 18, each leg 18, groin 1.
Infant: head 18, front trunk 18, back 18, each arm 9, each leg 13.5 (often rounded to 14), groin 1. Older child: head about 12, each leg about 16.5. Charts vary by text.
Patient's palm with fingers is about 1% of body surface area. Use for scattered/small burns.
Full-thickness over 10% or partial over 30% BSA (typical text); burns of face/airway, hands, feet, genitalia; circumferential; inhalation, electrical; with trauma; under 5 or over 55.
Singed nasal hair, soot in mouth/nose, hoarseness, stridor, burns of face, carbonaceous sputum. Consider early airway support.
Stop the burning, remove jewelry/clothing not stuck, cool briefly with room-temp water (not ice), cover dry sterile, prevent hypothermia.
Brush off dry powder first, then flush with copious water at least 20 min. Protect yourself (PPE). Remove contaminated clothing.
Ensure power is off/scene safe; entrance and exit wounds; internal damage is worse than it looks; expect dysrhythmias/cardiac arrest, so have the AED ready. ECG monitoring is ALS.
Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion; SpO2 may read falsely normal. Treat with 100% oxygen.

cards.front: ACS field triage 2021: Red criteria, mental status and vitals
cards.back: Motor GCS under 6 (can't follow commands); RR under 10 or over 29; SpO2 under 90%; SBP under 90 or HR over SBP (age 10-64); SBP under 110 (65+); SBP under 70 + 2 x age (0-9).

cards.front: ACS field triage 2021: Red criteria, injury patterns
cards.back: Penetrating head/neck/torso/proximal limb; skull deformity; spine injury with new deficit; flail chest; pelvic fx; 2+ proximal long-bone fx; mangled/pulseless limb; tourniquet-needed bleed.

cards.front: ACS field triage 2021: Yellow criteria, mechanism of injury
cards.back: Ejection; intrusion over 12 in at occupant site or 18 in anywhere; death in same compartment; unrestrained child 0-9; fall over 10 ft (all ages); pedestrian/cyclist/rider thrown or run over.

cards.front: ACS field triage 2021: Yellow criteria, EMS judgment
cards.back: Low-level fall with head impact (age 5 or under, or 65+); anticoagulant use; suspected child abuse; pregnancy over 20 weeks; burns with trauma; special needs. Follow local destination plan.
Red immediate, yellow delayed, green minor (walking wounded), black deceased/expectant.
RR over 30 = red. Radial pulse absent or cap refill over 2 s = red. Cannot follow simple commands = red. Not breathing after opening the airway = black.
Apneic after airway opened: pulse present = 5 rescue breaths (still apneic = black, breathing = red); no pulse = black. RR under 15 or over 45, no pulse, or P/U on AVPU = red.
Painful muscle spasms after exertion in heat; skin moist. Treat: rest in cool, oral fluids/electrolytes if alert.
Heavy sweating, pale cool clammy skin, weakness, dizziness, nausea, normal or slightly high temp. Cool, fluids if alert, may need IV by ALS.
Core temp over 104 F (40 C), hot skin (may be dry or sweaty), altered mental status or seizures. Life threat: rapid cooling, transport.

cards.front: Heat stroke vs exhaustion key difference
cards.back: Altered mental status and very high temperature = heat stroke. Cool aggressively (ice packs groin/axilla/neck, cold water immersion if possible).
Core 90-95 F (32-35 C): shivering, cold skin, pale, goosebumps, some confusion.
Core 82-90 F (28-32 C): shivering stops, confusion, slow pulse and respirations, stumbling, slurred speech.
Core under 82 F (28 C): unresponsive, rigid, very slow pulse; may appear dead. Check pulse longer than usual: 30-60 s in many texts (per local protocol). Not dead until warm and dead.
Handle gently (VF risk), remove wet clothes, insulate, passive warming, active warming per protocol, avoid rubbing limbs, no alcohol.
Superficial: white waxy skin, numbness, soft. Deep: hard, cold, blotchy white/gray/blue, blisters.
Remove wet clothing and jewelry, loosely cover with dry dressings, do not rub or break blisters, do not rewarm if refreezing is possible.
Cold, wet, nonfreezing exposure; swollen, pale, painful. Dry and rewarm gently.
Hypoxia is the problem: open airway and give rescue breaths first once safe, then CPR with ventilations if no pulse. Spinal precautions only if diving/trauma is suspected.
Cold water may preserve survival; continue resuscitation per protocol.
Transport even if the patient seems fine: lung problems (pulmonary edema, hypoxia) can develop hours later. 'Secondary' and 'dry' drowning are outdated terms.
Keep calm and still, limb about heart level (per local protocol), remove rings, mark swelling edge and time, rapid transport. No tourniquet, ice, cutting or suction.
Fang marks, pain, swelling, ecchymosis, weakness, metallic taste, bleeding.
Neurotoxin: minimal local signs; delayed weakness, drooping eyelids, respiratory failure. Remember 'red on yellow kills a fellow'.
Scrape out stinger (don't squeeze venom sac), wash, cold pack. Watch for anaphylaxis.
Muscle cramps/rigidity (abdominal), severe pain, sweating. Antivenom at hospital.
Painless bite then necrotic ulcer over hours/days; fever, chills.
Remove with tweezers close to skin; Lyme disease: bull's-eye rash, fever. Rocky Mountain spotted fever: rash wrists/ankles.
Arterial gas embolism: rapid ascent with breath-holding; sudden stroke-like signs, chest pain within minutes. Recompression needed.
Nitrogen bubbles after rapid ascent: joint pain, rash, fatigue, onset hours later. Transport to hyperbaric chamber.
High-concentration oxygen, position supine (left-side/head-down is no longer routine; per local protocol), keep warm, transport toward hyperbaric care. If flown: low cabin altitude.
Headache, nausea, fatigue above 8,000 ft; severe forms HAPE (lungs) and HACE (brain). Descend, oxygen.
Make scene safe, triage reverse: treat those in apparent arrest first. Look for burns, cardiac arrest, spinal and eardrum injury.

cards.front: Heat stroke: field cooling methods and when to stop
cards.back: Remove clothing; cold-water immersion is fastest if available. Otherwise wet the skin and fan, with ice packs at neck, armpits, groin. Stop near 102 F (39 C), per local protocol.
Conduction (direct contact), convection (moving air/water), radiation, evaporation (sweat/wet skin), and respiration.
Infants, elderly, chronic illness, alcohol/drug use, medications, prolonged exposure.
Balance, Eyes (vision loss), Face droop, Arm drift, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911.
Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech. One abnormal finding = high stroke probability.
Ischemic: clot blocks vessel (about 87%). Hemorrhagic: vessel bursts, bleed. Both need rapid transport to stroke center.
Last known well time, glucose check (rule out hypoglycemia), oxygen if hypoxic, pre-alert stroke center.
Transient ischemic attack: stroke symptoms resolving within minutes to 24 hours. Warning sign; still transport.
Phases: aura, tonic (stiff), clonic (jerking), postictal state. Lasts few minutes.
Period after seizure: confusion, drowsiness, headache, can last 5-30 minutes or longer.
Seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness. Life threat: support airway, rapid transport.
Protect from injury, nothing in the mouth, do not restrain, suction/airway after, oxygen, check glucose, note duration.
Seizure with fever in child about 6 months to 5 years; usually brief and generalized. Transport; cool without ice.
Epilepsy, hypoglycemia, head trauma, fever, drugs/alcohol withdrawal, stroke, eclampsia, hypoxia.
Brief loss of consciousness due to decreased brain blood flow. Look for cardiac or other causes.
AEIOU-TIPS: Alcohol, Epilepsy/Electrolytes, Insulin, Overdose/Oxygen, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychosis, Stroke.
Rapid onset: anxious, diaphoretic, pale cool skin, tremors, tachycardia, hunger, confusion, seizures. Glucose under about 70 mg/dL.
Slow onset: warm dry skin, polyuria, polydipsia, fruity (acetone) breath, Kussmaul respirations, nausea, abdominal pain, dehydration.
Commonly under 70 mg/dL with symptoms (protocols vary, about 60-70). Give oral glucose only if the patient is awake and can swallow; otherwise airway support and ALS.
Only if awake, able to swallow and protect the airway. Typical dose 15 g (one tube) between cheek and gum; repeat per local protocol. Contraindicated if unresponsive.

cards.front: Diabetic: 'cold and clammy' vs 'hot and dry'
cards.back: Cold and clammy = give sugar (hypoglycemia). Hot and dry = hyperglycemia; transport and treat per protocol.
Severe life-threatening allergic reaction with airway/breathing/circulatory involvement.
Hives, swelling of face/lips/tongue, wheezing, stridor, hypotension, vomiting, tachycardia.
0.3 mg for patients over about 30 kg (66 lb).
0.15 mg for children about 15-30 kg (33-66 lb). A 0.1 mg device exists for infants 7.5-15 kg; under 15 kg follow medical direction/local protocol.
Lateral mid-thigh (vastus lateralis), through clothing if needed; hold 3 seconds (follow device). Record time; may repeat per protocol.
Tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, pallor, headache, hypertension.
Albuterol relieves wheezing in asthma/COPD; check expiration, shake, spacer, patient's own prescription with medical direction.
Asthma: reversible wheezing, younger, triggers. COPD: chronic, smoking, barrel chest, productive cough. Both: oxygen, bronchodilator.
Acute pulmonary edema/CHF or COPD with respiratory distress; contraindicated if unresponsive, vomiting, or hypotensive.
Patient's own prescription, medical direction, SBP above local minimum (commonly 100; some use 90), no ED drugs in 24-48 h. 1 SL dose every 5 min, max 3; recheck BP each time.
162-324 mg chewed (2-4 baby aspirin of 81 mg) for suspected ACS if no allergy, active GI bleeding or other contraindication; per local protocol.
Ingestion, inhalation, absorption (skin), injection.
Binds ingested toxins; use only per medical direction. Not for acids/alkalis/alcohol; patient must be alert.
Pinpoint pupils, decreased mental status, slow respirations (respiratory depression). Treat with ventilation and naloxone.
Opioid antagonist; intranasal commonly 2-4 mg (per local protocol), may repeat in 2-3 min. Support ventilations first.
Dilated pupils, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis (cocaine, amphetamines).
Decreased mental status and respirations, slurred speech (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates).
SLUDGE/DUMBELS: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis; pinpoint pupils. Decontaminate; ALS atropine.
'Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter': fever, dry skin, dilated pupils, delirium.
Periumbilical pain moving to right lower quadrant (McBurney's point), nausea, fever, guarding.
Rigid board-like abdomen, rebound tenderness, patient lies still with knees flexed.
Tearing abdominal/back pain, pulsatile mass, hypotension, syncope; older male smoker. Rapid transport, gentle palpation.
Sudden tearing chest/back pain, unequal BP or pulses in arms; can mimic MI.
Right upper quadrant to right shoulder/scapula.
Left upper quadrant to left shoulder (Kehr's sign).
Epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea; often after alcohol or gallstones.
Flank pain radiating to groin, restless patient, hematuria.
Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena (black tarry stool), hematochezia. Treat for shock.
Visceral: dull, poorly localized, crampy. Parietal: sharp, constant, localized (peritoneal irritation).
Chest pressure/pain radiating to arm/jaw, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea. Women/diabetics/elderly may have atypical symptoms.
Angina: relieved by rest/nitro in about 5-15 minutes. MI: lasts over 15-20 minutes, not relieved by rest/nitro.
Left: crackles, dyspnea, orthopnea, frothy sputum. Right: JVD, peripheral edema, ascites.
Power on, attach pads, analyze, clear, shock if advised; resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes.
Compressions 100-120/min, depth at least 2 inches (5 cm), full recoil, minimal interruptions. Ratio 30:2 (1 or 2 rescuers).
Behavior unacceptable to patient, family, or community; can be due to medical cause: always rule out hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, drugs.

cards.front: Hyperactive delirium with severe agitation (formerly 'excited delirium')
cards.back: Extreme agitation, hyperthermia, sweating, tachycardia, pain tolerance, paranoia. Sudden death risk: avoid prone restraint, monitor airway/breathing, request ALS and police.
Reasonable force, adequate help (4-5), supine or lateral, never prone/hobble, reassess airway and circulation, document, follow protocol.
Ask directly about thoughts and plan; secure scene; never leave patient alone; transport all.
Calm, honest, nonjudgmental, keep distance, avoid sudden moves, don't argue or lie.
Older adults may have blunted responses: normal-looking BP may be abnormal for them; beta-blockers hide tachycardia.
MI/infection may present as weakness, confusion or falls rather than classic pain.
Consider syncope, medications, infection, poor vision; high risk for hip fracture and head bleeds (anticoagulants).
Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating, medical cause. Dementia: gradual, chronic memory decline.
Many medications raise risks for interactions, falls, and toxicity; bring/collect med list.
Unexplained injuries, poor hygiene, malnutrition, fearful caregiver interaction. Mandatory reporting per local law.
Infection plus fever/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension, warm or mottled skin. Early recognition and pre-alert.
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxia; risk: immobilization, surgery, clotting, pregnancy.
Severe BP elevation with headache, vision change, confusion, chest pain or neurologic signs.
Fluid overload/hyperkalemia risk; do not take BP or IV in fistula arm.
Stage 1: dilation (onset to full cervical dilation). Stage 2: expulsion (full dilation to birth). Stage 3: placental delivery.
Crowning, urge to push/bear down, contractions 2 minutes or less apart, bloody show, rupture of membranes.
Baby's head visible at vaginal opening during contraction. Prepare for delivery; do not delay delivery to transport.
Frequency: start of one to start of next. Duration: start to end of one. Active labor: 2-3 minutes apart, 45-60 s each.
Due date, first baby?, prior births/C-section, contractions timing, water broke, urge to push, bleeding, multiples, prenatal care.
Gravida: number of pregnancies. Para: number of births (viable deliveries).
Support the head, check for cord around neck, suction mouth then nose only if airway is obstructed, guide head down for upper shoulder then up for lower; support the slippery newborn.
Gently slip over head or shoulder; if too tight, clamp in two places and cut between.
Vigorous newborn: wait at least 60 s (AHA 2025). First clamp about 6 in from baby (texts vary, 4-10 in), second 2-3 in from the first; cut between. Follow local protocol.
Usually within 30 minutes; do not pull on cord. Transport placenta in bag with mother.
Massage uterus (fundus) firmly, place newborn to breast, treat shock, rapid transport.
About 500 mL is normal; more than that is excessive.
Buttocks or feet first; high risk. Do not pull; support and rapid transport; if head stuck, make airway space with fingers (V-shape).
Cord appears in vagina before baby. Mother knee-chest or Trendelenburg, gloved hand lifts presenting part off cord, keep cord moist, rapid transport.
Arm or leg first; cannot be delivered in field; rapid transport, knee-chest.
Expect more babies; call ALS; keep each baby warm; second delivery usually quick; increased bleeding risk.
Placenta covers cervix: painless bright red vaginal bleeding in third trimester.
Placenta separates early: painful bleeding (may be hidden), rigid tender uterus, fetal distress; trauma/hypertension risk.
Previa = painless, bright red. Abruption = painful, dark, rigid uterus.
Implantation outside uterus (usually tube): lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, shock, missed period; life-threatening.
After 20 weeks: hypertension, headache, visual changes, edema, upper abdominal pain.
Seizures in pregnancy/preeclampsia. Care: left lateral, airway, oxygen, dim lights, rapid transport, ALS (magnesium).
Uterus compresses inferior vena cava when lying flat after about 20 weeks; place mother on left side or tilt uterus left.
Treat the mother first; high-flow oxygen, left lateral tilt on backboard, fetal loss risk from placental abruption.
Loss before 20 weeks: cramping, bleeding, tissue. Care: pads (no packing), keep tissue, emotional support.
Increased heart rate and blood volume, decreased BP in 2nd trimester, increased respiratory rate.
Pads, not packing; save clots/tissue; treat shock; ask about pregnancy.
Preserve evidence (do not wash, change, or clean), be nonjudgmental, privacy, same-gender provider if possible, notify law enforcement per protocol.
Infection of female organs: lower abdominal pain, fever, discharge.
Appearance (color), Pulse, Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), Respirations. Each scored 0-2.
0 blue/pale all over, 1 pink body with blue extremities, 2 completely pink.
0 absent, 1 under 100/min, 2 at 100/min or more.
0 no response, 1 grimace/weak cry, 2 cough, sneeze or strong cry.
0 limp/flaccid, 1 some flexion of extremities, 2 active motion.
0 absent, 1 slow/irregular/weak cry, 2 good strong cry.
Scored at 1 and 5 minutes. 7-10 normal, 4-6 moderately depressed, 0-3 severely depressed. Do not delay resuscitation to score.
Dry, warm (wrap, cover head), position airway, suction mouth then nose only if secretions obstruct, stimulate by rubbing back/flicking feet.
Apnea/gasping or heart rate under 100 after drying, warming and stimulating: BVM ventilations at 40-60 breaths/min with room air first. Recheck heart rate after 30 s.
Heart rate under 60 despite at least 30 s of effective ventilation: 3:1 ratio (90 compressions + 30 breaths per min), two thumbs on lower third of sternum, depth 1/3 of chest.
Heart rate about 120-160, respirations 40-60, temp maintained; acrocyanosis (blue hands/feet) is common.
Green/brown fluid; if baby not vigorous suction and resuscitate per protocol; avoid routine deep suctioning.
Appearance (tone, interactiveness, consolability, look/gaze, speech/cry), Work of breathing, Circulation to skin. Done from across the room.
Infant 100-160, toddler 90-150, preschool 80-140, school age 70-120, adolescent 60-100. Approximate: ranges vary by textbook.
Infant 30-60, toddler 24-40, preschool 22-34, school age 18-30, adolescent 12-16. Approximate: ranges vary by textbook.
Infant 70-95, toddler 80-100, preschool 80-100, school age 80-110, adolescent 110-130 (tables vary). Hypotension age 1-10: SBP under 70 + 2 x age in years.

cards.front: Signs of respiratory distress in children
cards.back: Nasal flaring, retractions (intercostal/supraclavicular), grunting, head bobbing, seesaw breathing, stridor.
Altered mental status, slowing or irregular respirations, poor tone, cyanosis. Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise: ventilate with BVM.
Viral, gradual onset, barky seal-like cough, stridor on inspiration, low fever, 6 months to 3 years; humidified O2, calm child.
Bacterial; rapid onset, high fever, drooling, tripod position, muffled voice, no cough. Keep calm, do not examine throat, oxygen blow-by, rapid transport.
Croup: barky cough, no drooling, gradual. Epiglottitis: drooling, toxic ill, sudden, minimal cough.
Wheezing and respiratory distress in infants in winter; nasal suction, oxygen.

cards.front: Foreign body airway obstruction: infant vs child (AHA 2025)
cards.back: Infant: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts. Child: 5 back blows alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts (2025 change; older texts say thrusts only). Unresponsive: start CPR.
1 rescuer 30:2; 2 rescuers 15:2; 100-120/min; depth 1/3 of chest (about 1.5 in infant, 2 in child). Infant: 2 thumbs-encircling or heel of 1 hand (AHA 2025: no 2-finger).
Length-based tape (Broselow) for equipment/doses. Oral airway: corner of mouth to earlobe/angle of jaw; in children insert tip-down with a tongue depressor, without rotating.
Larger tongue, narrower airway, floppy trachea, belly breathers; use padding under shoulders to neutral/sniffing position.
Sudden unexplained death of infant under 1 year, usually during sleep, peak 2-4 months. Attempt resuscitation unless obvious death signs; support family.
Typically 6 months to 5 years with rapid temp rise; usually under 5 minutes. Protect airway, remove excess clothing (no ice or cold baths), transport.
Sunken fontanelle/eyes, no tears, dry mucosa, fewer diapers, lethargy, delayed cap refill.
Injury inconsistent with story, delay seeking care, multiple bruises at different stages, patterned marks, shaken baby signs. Report per law.
Use a pediatric burn chart (head is a larger % of BSA); large heavy head makes head injury likely in falls; pad under the torso to keep the spine neutral during SMR.
Common in sick infants; check glucose; altered mental status or poor feeding.
Common household toxins; call poison control 1-800-222-1222 and get substance, amount, time.
